newsitem.title: LEBANON: Beirut bank merger sets consolidation trend.
newsitem.headline: Beirut bank merger sets consolidation trend.

text.p: Societe Generale Libano-Europeene de Banque (SGLEB), one of Lebanon's top 10 banks, said on Tuesday it had agreed to acquire Banque Geagea, a small family-owned bank, in a takeover likely to set off a consolidation trend among Lebanese banks.
A bank official said SGLEB signed a contract on July 3 to acquire Banque Geagea for about $4.5 million, comprising $3 million for its banking licence and the balance for its assets.

It was the first takeover of a financially sound Beirut bank in recent years and was carried out in line with the central bank efforts to promote the rationalisation of Lebanon's overcrowded banking sector, the official said.
"It's a first, the first sound bank getting merged," he told Reuters. "SGLEB is doing the merger to facilitate the restructuring of the Lebanese banking system in harmony with central bank policy.
"We may get more," he added.

He said under a 1993 law on bank mergers, Societe Generale Libano-Europeene de Banque, which is 50 per cent owned by Societe Generale France and 50 per cent by the Sehnaoui group, a Lebanese family holding, would receive a soft loan from the central bank to pay for Banque Geagea's licence.
Lebanon's 72 active banks include several small, under-capitalised family concerns like Banque Geagea which face problems raising funds to meet capitalisation targets set by the central bank.

The official said nearly 10 smaller banks were likely to disappear soon -- either in takeovers like Banque Geagea or by losing their licences if they failed to meet their target by the end of the year.
Banque Geagea's assets totalled only about one percent of SGLEB's assets of 1.921 billion Lebanese pounds ($1.237 billion) at end 1996, the official said.
It has three branches and 30 employees compared with SGLEB's 30 branches, 642 employees and 5.7 percent market share.
"None of Banque Geagea's directors will be taken onto the board of SGLEB because we are acquiring the assets and liabilities and not exchanging shares ," the official said.

The acquisition requires the approval of the Bank of Lebanon, but Governor Riad Salameh told Reuters the central bank was in favour of the takeover and expected more of the same by the end of the year.
"We look favourably on such acquisitions...I think there will be some more," Salameh said by telephone.
"The fact that one bank is acquiring another bank in good health is a first in the sense of letting the sector consolidate and turn out with bigger capitalised banking entities," he said.

Under a June 5, 1996, central bank regulation banks must have 10 billion Lebanese pounds ($6.5 million) capital for head office and 250 million pounds ($162,000) for each branch by end 1997 while maintaining an eight percent Cooke liquidity ratio.
"Many of the small banks would require heavy capitalisation to reach this size," the SGLEB official said.
"To maintain the Cooke ratio they would need to get fresh money all the time, and they could not always manage to do this in the long run," he said.

Owners of small Beirut banks have been notoriously reluctant to go to the market for funds because they do not want to lose control, but Salameh said those which fail to meet the capitalisation target could lose their licences.

"The deadline is December 1997 and after this a bank that does not meet the requirement will have to face some disciplinary action," he said. Asked if this meant the loss of licence, he said: "That would be the inclination."
However, the SGLEB official said if the banks agreed to takeovers, they would at least get $3 million for their licences.
"This will reduce the number of banks softly through mergers -- smoothly, softly and calmly," he said.
